title: Whether the personal subsistence of the Logos is communicated to his human nature; and whether they speak rightly who say Christ's humanity subsists everywhere by that subsistence
english: Article XII. Whether the personal subsistence of the Logos is communicated to his human nature; and whether they speak rightly who say Christ's humanity subsists everywhere by that subsistence.

1. From the common saying that the hypostasis, or subsistence, of the Logos is communicated to Christ's flesh, two corollaries are drawn. First, the Ubiquitarians gather from it that omnipresence — indeed all the properties of the Logos — are communicated to the human nature. The reason of the consequence is that the hypostasis of the Logos does not really differ from its essence, and therefore not from its essential properties either: if therefore it is true that the hypostasis of the Logos is communicated to the flesh, it must also be granted that his properties are communicated to it in the same way. Second, some even among our own theologians, who think Christ's flesh can be said to subsist in every place by the subsistence of the Logos although it exists in one place alone, reason from the same foundation thus: the subsistence of the Logos is communicated to Christ's human nature; since therefore the subsistence of the Logos is infinite and is enclosed by the bounds of no place, Christ's flesh, by that subsistence communicated to it, can be said to subsist everywhere. This latter argument is more dangerous than the former, because it so greatly pleases certain Orthodox theologians that they profess that in this controversy concerning the local presence of Christ's flesh we differ from the Ubiquitarians only by a dispute about words, and by a merely verbal disagreement — which, whether it be true, let those judge who have more carefully considered the history of the colloquy of Mompelgart and the polemical writings of Beza and of Jacob Andreae on this matter.

2. In order, then, that those two arguments may be clearly dissolved, the verb 'to communicate' must be distinguished, and it must be taught in what sense Christ's subsistence is communicated to the flesh. It is therefore to be held that something is said to be communicated to another in three ways. First, both by inhering and by naming, in the way the odor of an apple is communicated to the hand; for that odor, at least the same in kind, inheres in the hand and denominates the hand — that is, is truly predicated of the hand. Second, something is communicated denominatively but not inhesively: in the way kings and emperors communicate the dignity of empire to their wives; for those wives are denominated Empresses and queens, not because they have imperial power or authority in themselves, but because their husbands have that authority. Third, something is communicated to another neither inhesively nor denominatively, but either effectively — in the way God is said to communicate himself to created beings, for those beings are called beings and goods by participation of the first being and the first good, as Zanchius speaks — or sustentatively, in the way a subject is communicated to its accidents, namely by sustaining them and receiving them into itself; or in some other similar mode. I say these are communicated neither denominatively nor inhesively, because God neither exists in creatures as an essential form, or as an accidental form in its subject, nor is predicated of them by true and affirmative predication; and the subject likewise neither inheres in its accidents nor denominates them, but on the contrary is denominated by them.

3. The hypostasis or subsistence of the Logos is communicated to his human nature in this third way: that is, it is communicated to it neither inhesively nor denominatively, but sustentatively only. The prior part of this assertion is declared thus: Christ's human nature (as Martinius well notes against Menzer) is void of all proper personal subsistence, and in no way subsists — that is, neither by itself nor by accident; or, to speak more plainly, neither by its own nature nor from the union. Therefore the subsistence of the Logos is communicated to it neither inhesively nor denominatively. The antecedent is proved: if Christ's humanity somehow subsists, it is somehow a suppositum or person, and therefore in some sense it will be true that Christ assumed a suppositum or a person; but the latter is absurd; therefore the former also. The connected claim is proved, because suppositum and subsistence reciprocate, so that every suppositum has subsistence, and everything that has subsistence is a suppositum. Someone will say: therefore Christ's flesh is plainly stripped of personality. It is answered that it is not stripped of personality in this sense, as if it were not united to some person — for it is united to the person of the Logos — but that subsistence properly and formally neither inheres in it nor can be attributed to it.

4. The same can also be demonstrated thus: if Christ's human nature subsists, either it subsists by itself — that is, has subsistence from itself — or it subsists insofar as it exists in the person of the Logos. The former will be admitted by no one; but neither is the latter free of manifest absurdity. Which is proved thus: Christ's flesh, insofar as it exists in the person of the Logos, has a certain mode of existing contrary to subsistence; therefore it does not subsist. The antecedent is proved: to be in another suppositum, and to subsist — that is, to be by oneself and outside every other suppositum — are two opposite modes of existing; but Christ's flesh, insofar as it exists in the person of the Logos, has the former mode of existing, that is, it exists in a suppositum; therefore it cannot have the latter, which is diametrically opposed to it.

5. The posterior part of our assertion is declared thus: the Logos graciously received and assumed our nature to his hypostasis, so that his hypostasis has the flesh intimately present to itself and bears it personally united to itself; but on the contrary the flesh clings in that hypostasis and is sustained. From which it follows that Christ's hypostasis, or personal subsistence, is rightly said to be communicated to the human nature sustentatively.

6. From this distinction of communication it is clear what is to be answered to either argument proposed at the threshold of this article. For since Christ's hypostasis is communicated to his humanity neither inhesively nor denominatively, it is evident that the Ubiquitarians cannot gather from the communication of the hypostasis of the Logos that his essential properties have been communicated to the assumed flesh, either inhesively or denominatively; and therefore all those inferences are to be denied by which, from that foundation, they conclude that Christ's flesh is omniscient, omnipresent, omnipotent, and so on. Likewise, since all those statements are false by which to subsist, or to have some personal being, is attributed to Christ's flesh — because, namely, it has no subsistence proper to itself, and no personal being, but a certain mode of existing contrary to them — it follows that Christ's humanity can neither be said to subsist everywhere by the subsistence of the Logos, nor to exist everywhere according to its personal being. Someone will say: Christ's human nature is joined to the person of the Logos, who is omnipresent and omnipotent; therefore the human nature can be called omnipresent and omnipotent personally. Answer: if that consequence is admitted, by equal reason these consequences also must be admitted: Christ's human nature is united to an infinite and eternal person; therefore it itself is infinite and eternal personally, or according to its personal being. Likewise, it is joined to that person who is God and Creator, and redeemer of the world; therefore these things belong to it personally.

7. Someone will ask here whether, just as the act of subsisting, so also the act of existing is to be removed from Christ's flesh. Answer: by no means. For Christ's flesh, although it does not subsist, nevertheless in truth has its own existence, distinct from the existence of the Logos, but dependent upon it. I say that it has an existence distinct from the existence of the Logos, because every created being has both an essence and an existence distinct from the essence and existence of the creator. I say that it has an existence depending on the existence of the Logos, because it cannot exist by itself and outside the person of the Logos.

title: On the diversity of material and immaterial forms
english: Second Exercise. On the origin of the soul and the propagation of sin.
Article I. On the diversity of material and immaterial forms.

So that we may settle the question of the soul's origin with a clear mind, I will first set down a few points about the kinds of forms, and about the different ways matter causes and receives the forms that enter it or are drawn out of it.

2. Hold first that effects made for a definite end — not at random or by chance — fall into three kinds, according as four causes, or three, or only two, concur in making them. Corporeal substances need all four: the two inward causes, matter and form, and the two outward ones, efficient cause and end, must join to give them the act of existing. Accidental forms or accidents, and every substantial form except the rational soul, are made by three — efficient, matter, and end. Angels and human souls are made by only two — efficient and end. Angels neither consist of matter and form nor exist in matter, so they can have no more than those two causes. Human souls, though they exist in matter, still do not consist of matter and form, and are not produced by the power of the matter they inhabit. Being spirits, they cannot be generated by any material power, as will be shown shortly; God creates them from nothing and introduces them into matter for the best end: his own glory and the eternal salvation of those persons.

3. Accidental forms such as whiteness or blackness need three causes if they are to have real being in the world. First, some end or purpose must stir and draw the efficient cause to act. Second, the efficient must apply its power — its active concurrence. Third, the matter-in-which, the subject of the whiteness, must concur passively and cooperate in giving that being to the accident: it does so by receiving the efficient's action that produces the whiteness, and by receiving and sustaining the whiteness itself. From these three the existence of whiteness and other accidents hangs — above all from the matter that receives them and, by passive concurrence, produces and sustains their being. Relative to efficient and end they depend only as to becoming; relative to matter or subject they depend both as to becoming and as to being. They cannot come to be without the concurrence of the matter in which they exist, nor keep the act of existing once that matter is gone. But if efficient and final cause are removed, an accident already produced can still persist in existence — as countless examples show.

4. Every substantial form except the human soul likewise needs three causes. For the form of a stone to exist in act, some end must move the efficient by what is called metaphorical motion; the efficient must, by its power in act, dispose the stone's matter to receive that substantial form; and matter, as a subjective cause, must concur in producing and sustaining the form. That form depends on matter for becoming, being, and operating: without the matter in which it exists it can neither come to be, nor be, nor operate. This dependence plainly shows that matter is a cause of the forms in it — not an active cause, but a passive, subjective one. Every dependence of one thing on another as on a prior in becoming and in being is a clear mark of causality. The human soul stands far otherwise. After a person's death it both exists and acts outside matter. Therefore it does not depend on matter for being or for operating, nor for becoming: matter cannot by any power or causal concurrence give being to a spiritual substance such as the rational soul, as will soon be proved, and so is in no way its cause. Hence the soul belongs with those things produced by only two causes — efficient and end. It is rightly called an immaterial form, independent of matter; every other form, substantial or accidental, is called material and dependent on matter. Fire's form cannot exist outside its matter, and without that matter it cannot heat or burn. A brute's form cannot exist without its matter — the body — and without that body it cannot sense or desire. The human soul not only exists outside matter after death; it also acts outside it, in understanding, willing, rejoicing, and grieving.

title: On matter's double causality and potency, and the eduction of forms from the potency of matter
english: Article II. On matter's double causality and potency, and the eduction of forms from the potency of matter.

1. First note that matter — the material cause — has a double causality: one toward the composite or mattered thing, another toward the forms that depend on it. Toward the composite its causality lies in constituting that composite as an essential part. Toward the forms that hang on it, its causality lies in concurring passively with the agent to give them being and to keep that being.

2. Second, matter's potency is of two kinds. One is only receptive, not causative; the other is both receptive and causative. Matter has the first kind toward the rational soul alone: it can naturally receive the soul into itself, but it cannot concur as a material cause in giving the soul being. It has the second kind toward every other form, essential or accidental: it can receive them and, by passive concurrence, cooperate with the agent in producing them.

3. Third, those philosophers go wrong who explain eduction by saying the form already exists in act in the matter before generation, only hidden under the confusion of potency, and that generation merely makes it manifest — as if actual being that was concealed simply becomes clear and is led out of matter's darkness into light. That account is bad. If the form already existed in act and united with matter before generation, the composite would already exist before it was generated — which is openly absurd, since matter and form existing in act and united necessarily yield the composite. Someone will object: if the form is not in the matter beforehand, how can it be educed or drawn out of it? Nothing is drawn out of what it is not in. Reply: the form is said to be educed from matter not from matter's substance, but from matter's causative potency. Before generation it does not exist in the substance of matter, yet it truly exists in matter's potency insofar as matter can produce it as a passive principle. To be in matter's causative potency is simply to be producible by matter as a passive principle.

4. Fourth, those also are wholly wrong who say forms exist in matter before generation according to an incomplete, imperfect being — by degrees of their entity — and through generation first attain complete, finished being in matter. That view makes a substantial form vary in intensity like an accident; and it absurdly packs into one and the same matter, all at once, every form that could be educed from it, total or partial — nearly infinite diverse substantial entities in one thing. Someone will object: if the form is nothing at all before generation, then every form comes from nothing and is therefore created. Reply: forms may be said to come from nothing if that means from no pre-existing part of themselves; not if it means from no pre-existing matter, which is the same as creation. Forms come to be from matter: matter concurs as a subjective cause in giving them being.

5. Fifth, it is also a bad account of eduction to say a form is educed from matter's potency merely because matter, before the form arrives, can receive it. If that were enough, every form without exception would be educible from matter's potency, since matter can receive any form — by a natural potency or an obediential one. Natural potency can be brought into act by a natural agent: wood's passive potency for heat is natural because fire can actualize it. Obediential potency cannot be actualized by a natural agent, but only by a superior agent of another order to which the matter is so subject that it must obey: wood or stone's potency for a statue's form is of this kind (art, not nature, actualizes it); so is the soul's potency for supernatural gifts — faith, hope, charity — which no natural power can bring into act, but only the creator's infinite power.

6. With that in place, eduction is easy to state. Nothing is educed from a thing except what was already in it. So only those forms are educed from matter's causative potency that, before they exist, are in that potency — producible by matter's passive concurrence. While they do not yet exist in act they can receive being from matter as a passive, receptive principle; when they begin to exist in act by the agent's active power and matter's passive power, they are rightly said to be educed from matter's causative potency, because they are no longer producible by it. What has once been caused is no longer in the cause's potency; it has been led from potentiality into actuality. A brute's form is truly educed from the causative potency of the seed's matter: before generation it was producible by that matter's passive power; through the generator's action it is produced and set outside that potency, and is producible by it again only if it loses the existence it now has. The human soul is produced in matter, yet it is not educed from matter's causative potency; it is induced into matter. It never lay in that potency, and matter never had a power, by passive concurrence, to give the soul being.

title: Whether the rational soul is from a translate
english: Article III. Whether the rational soul is from a translate.

1. The real question is this: is the rational soul educed from the potency of the seed's matter by seminal and prolific power, as plant and brute souls are — or does God produce it without any concurrence of pre-existing matter, creating it and infusing it into the body? Nearly all modern philosophers and theologians favor the second view, and rightly. I do not recall any contrary argument weighty enough to pull even a moderately practiced mind into the camp of those who say our souls are sown by parents in carnal generation and not created and infused by God. For immediate creation by God, Scripture's witness and philosophical arguments from known principles of nature both count. Leaving Scripture to the theologians — especially Junius on Genesis 1 — I offer reasons drawn from physics and metaphysics.

2. First: if the soul is generable, it is corruptible; but the consequent is absurd, so the antecedent is too. A form produced in generation by matter's concurrence depends on matter so that, once separated from what gave and kept its being, it must perish. Opponents reply that human souls are of themselves corruptible — the argument shows they depend on matter in becoming and being — yet will last forever because God has decreed to conserve them. Asked why the soul considered in itself is corruptible, they say that if God stopped conserving souls they would at once sink into nothing. That answer fails. When substances are divided into eternal and perishable, eternity does not mean independence from God's conserving influx; it means no creature can destroy them by a physical action. On that score angels, the heavens, and rational souls alike may be called incorruptible. Further, those who answer so cannot deny that the human soul cannot be destroyed by any physical or material action; from which I infer it also cannot be produced by any such action. Why can no physical action destroy it? Because it is a spiritual substance. For the same reason no material power can produce it: what is repugnant to a spirit in destruction is repugnant to it in production. Generation is a physical, material action — done in matter, by seminal virtue.

3. Second: God willed human souls to exist outside bodies after death, and brute souls to perish with their bodies. Therefore he gave the rational soul a nature independent of matter, so that by that nature it can exist outside corporeal matter. As to its nature, then, the soul is independent of corporeal matter.

4. Third: only that form is educed from matter's causative potency which comes to be with matter's passive concurrence giving it being. The seed's matter cannot by passive concurrence give being to the soul. Therefore the soul is not educed from matter's potency; God creates it and pours it into matter. The major is clear from what went before. The minor: no active power acts beyond its genus — it cannot produce what is of a higher nature and order. The soul exceeds the whole order of corporeal nature as a spiritual substance; no corporeal power can produce it. They reply that the material force in the seed cannot of itself make a spiritual substance, yet can, as instrument of the generating soul, be elevated beyond its species to produce a spirit — as a phantasm, a sensible material species, by the soul's power impresses intelligible (spiritual) images on the patient intellect. That evasion is empty. A created agent cannot, by a purely material instrument, produce something immaterial; and the prolific faculty in the seed is purely material. The case of intelligible species is different: the soul uses the agent intellect as a principal instrument to excite and elevate the phantasm. Universally, a material power cannot be the principal or sole instrument in producing a spiritual substance, though it may be a secondary instrument in producing a spiritual quality.

5. Fourth: opponents are driven to hard, absurd conclusions. To dodge these arguments they must deny that the soul is a spiritual substance, and allow that a physical action can destroy it unless God specially preserves it — claims that strip our soul of dignity and leave us no purchase against atheists from immortality. If the soul by nature depends on the body so that it cannot of itself exist outside it, how shall we persuade them it is immortal? The same conclusions slight divine wisdom: to say God willed souls to exist outside bodies and yet denied them a nature fit for that is to say he did not produce the soul wisely enough.

6. Fifth: though we hold that God creates the soul and infuses it, so that the parent does not give the child a soul, we can still maintain that a human generates a human as truly as a lion a lion or an ox an ox; and we can maintain that the natural hereditary corruption called original sin is passed from parents to children, and explain how. Nothing forces us into an opinion that contradicts the soul's nature and so deeply detracts from its dignity.

title: Whether and how a human being is truly said to generate a human being
english: Article IV. Whether and how a human being is truly said to generate a human being.

1. Philosophers and theologians who deny that the soul is translated through the seed, or drawn out of it, still disagree about what human generation is and in what action it consists. Some, pressed with the objection that the generator does not give the child the soul through which he is human and therefore does not generate a human, answer that a human generates a human by supplying the matter — the body — from which the human is made. That reply is cold and unworthy of a philosopher. It yields only that a human generates a human body, not the whole human — which is exactly what the objection proves. No philosopher has made substantial generation out to be the production or supply of matter; if producing a substance were supplying matter for it, the man who hands an artisan marble for a statue would be said to make the statue — which is absurd. To generate a human is to give a human being; and human being or nature is neither soul alone nor body alone. If it were either, separating soul from body would not destroy human nature. Human nature is the union of body and soul — truly consisting of both. If the generator only makes the body and does not make the child something consisting of soul and body, he does not truly give the child human being, and so does not truly generate a human.

2. Others, seeing the first reply fails, offer another almost as weak. They say a human truly generates a human because he not only gives a body but prepares the matter to receive the form, and by prolific virtue reaches the conjunction of soul and body that constitutes a human as a physical composite. They do not say the father joins the child's soul to the body by seminal virtue — that they leave to God who infuses the soul — but that he prepares the seed's matter for the human form, after which preparation the conjunction follows at once. On their view, generating is only a prior alteration and preparation of matter. Nearly all the older philosophers held this, nearly all the moderns, and most Roman theologians; the Coimbra commentators on De ortu 1 admit they once held it because it was common. It satisfies the objection no better than the first. Preparation of matter is a change in quality — alteration — and generation is not alteration: they are specifically different motions, one ending in quality, the other in substance. So generation is not preparation of matter. Generation is one simple change; that preparation is many alterations before the form arrives — dilating, solidifying, increasing or decreasing humor as the form requires. So it is an aggregate of changes, not generation. To generate is to give being; human being is consisting of soul and body. If God couples soul and body by infusion, God gives that being, not the generator. And a human is begotten in an instant, not gradually; so production is instantaneous, not successive.

3. A third reply says the generator gives neither matter alone nor preparation alone, but also a form — not the specific rational soul (God alone creates and unites that), but a vegetative and sensitive soul educed from the seed's potency. This is the weakest view of all. It makes a human generate not a human but a living thing and an animal. Human being is consisting of soul and body; if the child does not owe the father that he consists of a rational soul and a body, human nature has not been communicated by the father.

4. Rejecting these, we follow Du Val, Ruvio, and the Coimbra professors in a fourth account: a human truly generates a human even though God creates the soul — not by giving only a body, not by preparing the body for the soul, not by producing a vegetative or sensitive soul of the child in or from corporeal matter, but because from the generator comes the very action by which the rational soul is substantially united to the body and begins to inform, inhabit, and fill the whole matter of the body. On our view, human generation is that action by which, through prolific virtue, the soul is bound to the body by an essential bond.

title: Whether generation is placed in the production of the form or in the conjunction of form with matter
english: Article V. Whether generation is placed in the production of the form or in the conjunction of form with matter.

1. To make our view clear I will first show that the generator's action — speaking of generation in general — is placed in the conjunction of matter and form; then I will say something more particular about the action that unites soul and body. Generation of a composite is not production of matter. Matter properly so called is ungenerated and imperishable: only the creator can make it.f a creature produced prime matter from no pre-existing matter, it would create it; no creature creates, for creation needs infinite power. When air comes from fire, air generates air by turning fire into air; it does not produce new matter, but introduces a new form into matter already there.

2. Substantial generation is not production of matter, as shown; nor is it production of form. That is clear for those who hold souls are created by God, and no less clear against traducians. First: human nature is consisting of soul and body. By the action that unites soul to body — whether the soul is from God or from the father — a human becomes a composite of soul and body. So by that action the human receives human being and is produced: to produce a human is to bring it about that a being consisting of soul and body exists. Second: a physical composite is never produced anew — by generation or any other change — unless matter and form are newly joined into one per se. Yet a physical composite can be produced anew even when its form is not newly produced. So making a physical composite is joining matter and form rather than producing the form. Proof from the resurrection: then humans will be newly produced and newly receive human being by a true substantial production, though extraordinary; yet their soul is not newly produced — it has existed since creation — but only newly united with matter. So production of a physical composite is uniting form with matter, not producing form. If anyone denies that the resurrection is a true substantial production: to produce a corporeal substance is to give it being; God then truly gives the dead — who while dead lacked the being of a natural substance, not consisting of united matter and form — the full being of a natural body by making them consist of body and soul. So by that action God truly produces natural bodies. The action differs from ordinary generation, yet it is a true substantial production: to produce a substance is to confer being on what did not have substantial being before. Further: God can create an infant's soul some time before generation and then, in generation itself, join that soul to the body. So there can be true substantial generation without producing the form.

3. On the second point: those of our opinion on the soul's origin say that in brutes the seminal virtue has a double operation — educing the form from matter's potency, and uniting that form with the composite — operations diverse only in reason, because one and the same action educes the form and substantially unites it with matter. In humans, they say, the seminal virtue has only one principal action: uniting the form — the soul — with corporeal matter (lesser actions of preparing the body for the soul also proceed from it). So in producing a human there are two actions from two agents: creation of the soul, and uniting it with matter. Creation is God's alone. Uniting soul and body is not the human's alone — God cooperates — but the human's and God's together. And generation is placed in that uniting, not in another action: as shown, producing a composite is neither producing matter nor producing form, but uniting form with matter. In the same instant God creates the soul in the body, the generating human by seminal virtue substantially joins the God-created soul to the body. God's action terminates in the soul's being simply; the father's terminates not in that simple being but in the soul's being in the body — the union of soul and body.

4. To the objection that a human is human through the soul, so if the father does not give a soul he does not give human being: they reply that a human is human neither through soul alone nor through body alone, but through the whole nature or human essence. By uniting soul and body through seminal virtue the father gives the child to consist of soul and body, and so gives the nature and essence through which he is human. A thing is such a thing through the whole essence, not through one part — for essence is that through which a being is a being. The common saying that each thing is such through its form means: through the form as the principal part of the essence, not as an adequate reason (the adequate reason is having such an essence). Comparing the parts of a physical essence, a thing is such through form rather than matter; comparing either part with the whole essence, it is such through the essence rather than through either matter or form alone.

5. A serious difficulty remains. If God infuses the soul, as all of this opinion say, the conjunction of soul and body seems God's rather than the generator's — for what is infusion into corporeal matter but conjunction with matter? Some answer that God is said to infuse the soul not because he alone couples them, but because he does it through seminal virtue used as an instrument — not a necessary instrument (he can connect them of himself) but an ordinary one, as in every animal generation. Others more probably say God is said to infuse the soul not by substantially but by locally joining soul and body: he creates the soul in the body and by creating it in that place makes it locally present. In that same instant the seminal virtue connects the parts by a substantial bond. Local presence of the soul is far different from substantial union with matter: an angel clothed in an assumed body is locally present to that body, yet not substantially joined to it as form to its matter.

title: Whether the preceding doctrine abolishes the propagation of original sin
english: Article VI. Whether the preceding doctrine abolishes the propagation of original sin.

1. Those who deny that God immediately creates the human soul and hold instead that it is educed from the seed's potency commonly object that our doctrine abolishes original sin's propagation and leaves no way to explain how that sin passes from parents to children. To dissolve the cavil by the fact itself, I will name the quasi-integral parts of that sin and show how each is propagated.

2. Original sin has three parts. First: participation in the first parents' sin — the common sin of the whole human race. Second: lack of original justice, the defect of the gifts of intellect and will with which Adam and Eve were adorned before the fall. Third: propensity or inclination to evil. We not only lack the original justice that inclined us to good; when it was removed a contrary quality opposed to the law took its place and makes us prone to every baseness.

3. The first part is propagated neither through soul nor through body as such, but through natural generation — as lineage, nobility, and hereditary right are. Charles is heir because he is the king's son, and the king's son because the king begot him; he is noble because he descends by natural generation from noble parents. So Adam's sin is ours because we are his sons and heirs by natural generation from him. This coincides with those who say a God-created soul becomes corrupt and guilty through hypostatic union with the body: from that union comes the whole human who is Adam's successor and so guilty of Adam's disobedience.

4. Note three points carefully. First: this concerns only a successor begotten by natural generation — by the ordinary concurrence of male and female. Otherwise our Lord Jesus Christ would be guilty of Adam's sin, which is absurd and impious. Second: the blessed Virgin is necessarily guilty of Adam's sin. What makes us guilty of it is found in her; she descends from Adam as we do; therefore she is no less guilty than we.

5. Third: only the first human's sins pass to children, not later parents' sins. The first human received justice not for himself alone but for all his posterity: if he remained in it he would transmit it with nature; if he forsook it by sinning he would pour the stain with nature into all posterity. Later parents were not instituted under that law, so their sins — like their justice — are not propagated but remain singular and personal.

6. Parents transmit the second part — lack of original justice — negatively, as poor and ignoble parents transmit want and obscure lineage: children lack goods their parents cannot confer. So a newborn lacks original justice because the parents lack it and cannot communicate it. Why then do not faithful parents, somewhat restored by grace, transfuse those gifts? Because transmitting this gift to descendants was granted only to the first parents before the fall — not to later parents, nor even to Adam after he once sinned.

7. The third part is commonly said to be transmitted as leprosy is — through seed. Infection in a leper's seed is not leprosy formally and actually but only virtually, a hidden disposition toward leprosy. So spiritual infection in the seed is not sin actually and formally but a hidden disposition toward sin; thus a soul God creates in the body contracts vice from the body from the first, as in a foul place. The solid ground is the natural mutual sympathy — communication of passions and affections — between body and soul as substantial parts of one natural composite. When the body is badly affected, the soul is badly affected.

title: Objections against native corruption's propagation through parental seed are answered
english: Article VII. Objections against native corruption's propagation through parental seed are answered.

1. First objection: a body cannot act on a spirit by impressing a vicious quality; so concupiscence is not derived from body to soul. Pareus (from Augustine) answers that the soul contracts vice from vitiated flesh not wholly by nature but by God's hidden judgment for the first parents' fault — the body cannot naturally act on spirit, yet by the hidden justice of God's law it can happen. Others locate it not in flesh's action on soul but in natural concomitance between matter and form: as the soul communicates life and sense to the body, so the body's dispositions are communicated to the soul (a soul infused into a badly disposed body becomes dull, as in the naturally foolish — Esthius). Zanchi adds: infection comes from conjunction with the body not by physical action but by God's just ordinance — as Adam's justice would have flowed to children if he had not sinned, so when he sinned nature's corruption flows from him as head into all, through seed as the vehicle of the stain.

2. Alexander of Hales and Bonaventure: the soul is vitiated in an unclean body not by flesh truly acting on spirit, but because flesh stripped of original rectitude and rebellious to reason draws the mind down and warps it. Pareus: imagine the body prone to evils and unfit as an organ for good acts; the soul, robbed of original purity, follows that vicious temperament (Hommius likewise).

3. Second objection: if God thrusts a pure soul into so impure a prison he acts cruelly — which is blasphemous to say, so the premise is absurd. We concede the whole: we do not say God sends a just, pure soul into an impure body (that would make souls just before infusion — refuted in Art. VIII). Press: God infuses a soul that of itself has no sin into a contagious body, so he acts unjustly. Deny the consequence. Injustice is doing what equity binds one to do the contrary of. God is not bound to give Adam's children — who sinned in Adam and merited eternal death — pure bodies before infusion; by the threat In the day you eat you shall die he is bound not to purge them.

4. Third: the cause of a cause is cause of the caused; God causes union; union causes the soul's sin; so God causes sin. Zanchi: union is a cause of sin only per accidens — had Adam not sinned, God would have joined souls and bodies without sin following. Further: God creates souls in the body; parents by prolific virtue substantially unite them. Having souls in bodies is from God; having them created in impure bodies is from the fall. The rule applies to causes per se, not per accidens. God causes his law; the law causes sin per accidens (Rom 7:8–14); yet God is not the cause of sin.

5. Fourth: what the body lacks it cannot use to infect the soul; but soul-proper sin (ignorance, aversion from good) is not in the body. Answer: as leprous seed produces leprosy without having leprosy formally — only a hidden disposition — so flesh can infect the soul with only a virtual disposition toward sin. What the body has neither formally nor virtually cannot infect; what it has virtually can.

6. Fifth: in Adam sin was first in the soul and passed to flesh, not reverse; so in his children the soul is first-sufferer. Pareus: the order in vice from free choice differs from the order in vice generated from flesh. Or: the soul is still first-sufferer actually and formally, though the body has the disposition virtually first. Those who put original sin actually and formally in the seed before the soul are absurd: habit and privation concern the same subject; original justice cannot be in seed, so neither can its privation. If seed had sin formally, seed would have a law, face eternal damnation, and be able to be redeemed, repent, and believe — absurdities Keckermann says can scarcely be outdone.

title: Several questions on the propagation of original sin are proposed and answered
english: Article VIII. Several questions on the propagation of original sin are proposed and answered.

1. First: how can original sin be translated when its subject, the soul, is not? Esthius: accidents often pass by affection or infection without the subject's passing — as heresies, errors, and vices spread from one to many without the soul's passing. That holds for an accident the same in species, not in number; a numerically identical accident requires its subject's transfer too. Some philosophers similarly say that when odor passes into a handling hand, the fruit's subtler parts that proximately bear the odor also pass.

2. Second: Did the soul sin in Adam's loins? Distinguish. As to being simply, the soul was not in Adam's loins and did not sin there. As to being in the body and union with it, it can be said to be drawn from Adam, to have been in his loins, and to have sinned: the whole human was in Adam's loins by natural generation and so is guilty of Adam's sin; the whole human is not bound to punishment unless both soul and body are.

3. Third: Does God impress original sin by creating and infusing the soul? No. In creating the soul God confers neither justice and holiness nor impurity and propensity to evil, but only a spiritual essence and properties that flow from it. He does not breathe the lethal poison of concupiscence — he will not be evil's author — nor does he infuse holiness and justice, for the soul is created as a constitutive part of Adam's son and successor, to whom God is not bound to give spiritual gifts (Junius on Gen 2).

title: Lighter arguments against the creation and infusion of the soul are dissolved
english: Article IX. Lighter arguments against the creation and infusion of the soul are dissolved.

1. Objection: God finished creation in six days and rested (Gen 2; Exod 20), so new souls are not now created. Answer: after the sixth day he ceased creating new species, not new individuals. Souls he now creates differ from Adam's first-created soul in number, not in species.

2. Genesis 5: Adam begot a son in his image; a son is the father's image according to the soul; so Adam begot according to the soul. Answer: the likeness is chiefly of the whole person consisting of soul and body, not of the soul alone. Adam begot not only a like son but the very person composed of soul and body in which that likeness chiefly consists (Esthius).

3. Genesis 46: seventy souls went out from Jacob's thigh — supposedly translation by seed. Answer: souls stand synecdochically for humans. Or: souls went out from Jacob's thigh not as to simple being but as to existence in the body and union with it; the seed's virtue effected that union.

4. If generating does not produce a rational soul, humans are worse off than brutes and plants that produce their own vegetative and sensitive souls. Esthius: humans are better off even in generating, because generative power reaches the union of the noblest form with matter. It is dignity to have a soul so excellent that no natural power can produce it — which is why even angels have no generative power.

5. If the father generates only the body, he does not generate the whole human but the less noble part. Deny the sequel. Mary did not beget Christ's deity yet truly begot the whole Christ; fire from wood generates fire's form, not its matter, yet generates that whole fire (Aristotle: generation is change of the whole). Distinguish the whole human from the whole of the human: the father generates the whole human — all the parts.

6. If God creates each soul of whoever is begotten, he cooperates with fornicators and adulterers. Answer: God cooperates with natural generation, good of itself and nature's work — not with the vice by which they complete generation against his law.

title: Whether a more convenient account of the traduction of concupiscence can be given than we gave as original sin's third part
english: Article X. Whether a more convenient account of the transmission of concupiscence can be given than we gave as original sin's third part.

1. Those who reject the common view — that the soul is infected from a body disposed to sin — fall into four classes. First: Traducians, who attack soul-creation and claim their foundations yield a far safer account of sin's traduction than ours. Of them later.

2. Second class: they say a human naturally consists of flesh and spirit, sharing nature with beasts and with angels. By flesh he has a propensity to corporal, sensible good via sense and appetite; by spirit, to spiritual, intelligible good via intellect and will. From these contrary propensities, flowing necessarily from essential principles, they posit a fight between sense and reason and from it a huge difficulty of acting well.
3. Second, they say providence at creation added original justice as a golden bridle to remedy that diseased languor arising from the essential principles, holding sensitive appetite under reason.

4. Third, after the fall Adam lost that gift; so now concupiscence flows partly from the soul's essential constitution (sensitive and rational parts) and partly from lack of the original justice that subjected sense to intellect.

5. Our theologians rightly reject this. First: it underwrites the absurd dogma that concupiscence in the regenerate after baptism is not sin but a natural disease. Second: calling the sensitive appetite's rebellion natural insults God — as if the most holy God who hates sin impressed on human nature at creation a propensity to sin and to dishonest objects. Third: Bellarmine himself admits (Loss of Grace 5) that vicious concupiscence is also in the will, prone to honors, empty glory, and objects pleasant to sense and displeasing to reason — though it once held the contrary naturally. Here Bellarmine sticks until he takes our view of concupiscence in the regenerate.

6. Answering us (Grace of the First Human 7), Bellarmine says fleshly concupiscence was natural in the first state not as a good of nature but as a defect or disease following from matter's condition. So it is rightly called not from God, hate-worthy, evil, contrary to nature: it would have existed beside the author's intention if humans were created in pure naturals; and God had removed it, and by human fault it has place in us.

7. Crass and absurd. First: rebellion from nature yet not from God, nature's fount, is a contradiction. Second: God cannot produce what is contrary to his nature — goodness itself and propensity to good, contrary to propensity to evil. Third: on Bellarmine's view the supernatural gift of justice did not remove the sensitive appetite's natural propensity against reason's order (that would overturn its nature) but only restrained actual resistance. So Adam in integrity already had a propensity to evil in his appetite, though not yet broken into acts — and so was stained with original sin. What else is original sin than propensity to evil?

title: Two other opinions on the traduction of sin are considered
english: Article XI. Two other opinions on the traduction of sin are considered.

1. Next are the third and fourth classes that reject the common view of the soul's infection from the body. Third class: original sin is translated by natural generation alone, without infection of soul from body. Generation explains why we are guilty of Adam's sin, they say, but not our blindness, ignorance, and propensity to evil. So this view can account for the first part of original sin, not the second and third.

2. Fourth class: they agree with us on the first and second parts, but say the third is propagated not through itself but through the second — lack of original justice, to which it is necessarily joined. Why is a newborn guilty of Adam's sin? Because he is Adam's son by natural generation. Why does he lack original justice? Because parents lack it and cannot confer it. Whence propensity to evil? It necessarily follows lack of justice, as darkness follows lack of light.

3. This does not satisfy. Lack of original justice is mere privation and non-being; non-being cannot cause a real being such as propensity to evil, which imports a positive real habit (Molinaeus ch. 8). So lack of justice has no real positive causality for producing concupiscence. Objection: blindness causes a fall; lack of light causes wandering — and those are real. Answer: privation is not a positive efficient cause but a condition sine qua non, or a cause per accidens.

4. For readers who have not met Molinaeus: his first assertion — that the intellect destitute of original justice and not yet called by the word neither knows nor can know spiritual and supernatural goods while that state lasts — needs no proof. Bellarmine (Grace and Free Choice 6.1): all theologians, Pontifical and Evangelical, agree those mysteries of faith cannot be known without divine revelation.

5. His further claims do not prove concupiscence arises merely from lack of justice. Concupiscence is not only proneness to excessive love of earthly things from ignorance of heavenly ones; it is also proneness to despising revealed heavenly goods known from the word, and to doing what we know from God's word to be base. So Paul (Rom 7:22–23): I delight in God's law in the inner human, but see another law in my members rebelling and leading me captive under sin's law.

6. If fleshly concupiscence were only inordinate love of earthly things from ignorance of heavenly ones, it would not remain after the word's illumination and regeneration — yet experience and Scripture say it remains in the regenerate. So explaining the third part by mere lack of justice is to be rejected.

title: Those who attack the creation of souls disagree among themselves; three of their opinions on the soul's origin are refuted
english: Article XII. Those who attack the creation of souls disagree among themselves; three of their opinions on the soul's origin are refuted.

1. After defending the common view on the soul's origin and sin's propagation, I meant also to propose and confute the adversaries' traducian opinions — for readers who have not yet met Molinaeus. Because I seriously reject eduction of the rational soul from matter's potency, it seemed worthwhile to confute one by one every opinion on soul-traduction I remember reading or hearing.

2. First: Jacob Martini (Miscellanies 3.7) — the child's soul is from the father's by a translate in an uninvestigable, unknown way. Easy, but dishonest, and unworthy of so sharp a man. Against those who hide in that den: what no natural cause produces per se in any way known to us cannot be said to be produced by a natural cause in an unknown way; but no natural cause produces the rational soul in a known way; therefore not in an unknown way either. Seeking ignorance's hiding-place when physical causes cannot be assigned destroys the opinion rather than strengthens it.

3. Second: those who say the soul is educed from the seed's potency — which Meisner keenly defends and which is rightly rejected. His own arguments: an accident (seminal virtue) cannot produce so noble a substance; the soul is an immaterial form, so not in the seed before arrival; material forms are educed from matter's potency, but the soul is spiritual. As these strike eduction from matter, they also strike a material translate.

4. Third: the parent emits with the seed a particle of his soul, so the seed is actually animated when emitted; the child's soul comes by division and a kind of diminution of the father's. Meisner rightly judges this unsafe: it makes the soul divisible and therefore material and corruptible — for what is divided and diminished is quantitative and material.

title: Meisner's fourth opinion is refuted
english: Article XIII. Meisner's fourth opinion is refuted.

1. Meisner's fourth opinion agrees with the preceding that the soul is not educed from the seed's potency but translated from parent to offspring and infused with the seed into the womb, so the seed is actually animated as soon as emitted. It differs in holding that the soul in the seed is not cut off or partitioned from the father's soul but generated and produced anew by it. Meisner (p. 924): as soon as the parent transfers seed into the mother's womb, he transmits with it a soul — not his own or a part of it, but one like his own.

2. there are four ways something can come into being from something else: effectively (effect from efficient cause); materially (a small nail from a mass of iron); subjectively (educed from a subject's potency, as material forms from matter); constitutively (natural bodies from matter and form).

3. On Meisner's view the father's soul creates the child's. What produces from nothing creates; the father's soul produces the child's from nothing; so it creates and has infinite power. The child's soul is not from the father's by partition (Meisner admits); not subjectively educed from its potency (or it would exist in the father's soul as in a subject); not constitutively (the father's soul is not a constitutive part). So from nothing — creation by the father's soul — which is absurd.

4. The likeness from light is inept. Light is educed from matter's potency (Fonseca): no one doubts light is educed from air's potency; when another torch is brought to a shining one, flame is educed from the applied torch's matter.
5. A power to procreate like souls without eduction from matter would belong to the rational soul as such, not as vegetative — and that cannot be granted without creation.

6. Both parents emit seed (Scholastics on Sent. 3 — Scotus, Bonaventure, Major, Ockham, and others — and physicians from anatomy: Galen, Fernel, Lemnius, Vesalius, Laurentius). If both seeds are animated, two souls in one fused seed; if only one, why does generation not always follow when sufficiently disposed seed is emitted?

7. It is absurd that a true miracle should occur whenever a father emits sufficiently disposed seed and animation (hence generation) does not follow — yet that would follow on Meisner's view with nature's course miraculously held back.
8. Every rational thing is a human; seed actually animated by a rational soul would be a human before the body is formed — absurd.

title: Bright's fifth opinion is confuted
english: Article XIV. Bright's fifth opinion is confuted.

1. As I was finishing this disputation, Timothy Bright of Cambridge's On Health, Disease, and Death came to hand, with a new opinion on the soul's origin. He answers: neither the whole nor a part of the parents' mind is translated, nor is some accident a mind-rudiment. What then? A substance born from the soul — neither whole nor part — as an immortal seed of the soul, principle of the offspring's future soul. As corporeal seed cut from the parents' bodies is neither the body nor a member, so the soul is translated through a fertile soul-seed, not through the soul or a part of it. The integral soul is referred to the parents as received; but something seminal is shut out from soul as from body, and by the blessing of fertility goes forth into a rational immortal soul.

2. First confutation: that spiritual seed truly pre-existed in the parent's soul — real emission presupposes real inherence — yet it cannot really inhere there, so cannot be really emitted. Not as part in whole (Bright admits); not as accident in a subject (it is a substance); not as in a surrounding place or vessel (repugnant to the soul's spiritual nature).

3. Second: the spiritual seed comes from the whole father's soul, or a part, or nothing. Not from corporeal matter — it is spiritual, and Bright says it is born from soul not body. Not from the whole soul (the whole would convert into seed); not from a part (the soul is indivisible). So from nothing — which is creation.

4. Third: conversion of that seed into a soul is accidental or substantial. Not accidental: then it would differ from the soul only by degree of accidental perfection — an inchoate imperfect rational soul — contradicting Bright's claim that it is not actually a soul but a principle of a future soul. If substantial, it happens by abolishing the whole, or one part of the essence while the other remains.

5. Fourth: God could annihilate that seed and in the same instant produce a soul from nothing; then production belongs to God alone, not the father — a huge absurdity if their traducian doctrine is true.

6. Fifth: conversion cannot abolish one essential part while another remains. That would make the spiritual seed-substance corruptible and capable of substantial change like physical bodies; and would make it composed of physical matter and form or essential parts — for only of those is it true that when one is destroyed the other can remain in actual existence.

7. Sixth: if the spiritual seed converts into a soul, generation cannot occur without the seed's perishing; yet the seed's form (the soul) would remain, and substantial conversion requires the prior form's perishing. So Bright's opinion is no safer than the preceding.

title: All the adversaries' opinions on the translate have been confuted; none of them can explain sin's propagation more safely or easily than we who defend the creation of souls
english: Article XV. All the adversaries' opinions on the translate have been confuted; none of them can explain sin's propagation more safely or easily than we who defend the creation of souls.

1. Those who hold the soul from a translate, not created and infused by God, must say either that it is educed from the seed's potency by matter's passive concurrence, or produced by the father's soul without the seed's matter — there is no middle. The first was confuted in Arts. III and XII. The second splits four ways: the father's soul produces the child's from its whole substance, or a part, or a spiritual seed, or nothing. I confuted the first in Art. XII, the second and the from-nothing case in Art. XIII, the spiritual seed in Art. XIV. So no traducian opinion stands that is not absurd and against sound philosophy.

2. No Traducian explains original sin's propagation more safely or easily than we who defend soul-creation. Meisner's argument, even limited, is weak. They say: if God creates and infuses the soul, original sin cannot pass into it, because an accident does not pass from subject to subject. But Arts. VI–VII showed how each part propagates without soul-traduction: the first by natural generation as hereditary right; the second negatively, by justice parents cannot confer; the third by a virtual disposition in the seed through body–soul sympathy. Soul-creation does not abolish sin's propagation — it best reconciles it.

3. Traducians who want the soul materially translated fall into worse absurdities: they make the soul divisible and corruptible, or give the parent creative power, or invent an inexplicable spiritual seed. Safer and easier, with the catholic church and the sounder philosophers: God creates and infuses the soul, and original sin propagates as we have explained.
4. End of the Second Exercise. The Third follows — On Faith, Knowledge, and related questions.

title: On the firmness, certainty, and evidence of the mind's acts of assent
english: Third Exercise. On Faith, Science, and Opinion.
Article I. On the firmness, certainty, and evidence of the mind's acts of assent.

1. Every intellective habit has knowledge — or assent — as its proximate end: the mind assents to those propositions whose truth it perceives and cognizes. It is therefore worthwhile to premise something about the mind's assent, its affections, and its species, so that the diversity of our mind's acts may be understood.
2. Assent of the mind is the judgment by which the intellect judges some proposition true. The mind assents to "man is an animal" by embracing and approving it — that is, by judging it true.

3. Philosophers have marked three degrees of perfection in assent: firmness, certainty, and evidence. Opposed to them are three degrees of imperfection: infirmity or vacillation, uncertainty, and inevidence.

4. Firm assent is without hesitation, doubt, or fear of the opposite side. Infirm or vacillating assent is when the mind so assents that it doubts the proposition's truth, or at least somehow fears that by assenting it may err.

5. Certain assent rests on some certain or solid foundation, not on a light or fallacious reason. Uncertain assent is the contrary. Note carefully: for certainty it is required that the foundation on which the mind rests while assenting not only be certain in itself, but also appear such to the one who assents. Unless he knows that the reason on which he rests is certain, his assent will in no way be certain and stable.

6. Evident assent is when someone, by the force of his own sense or reason and apart from another's information or testimony, perceives that the proposition to which he assents is true. When I see Socrates standing near me and assent to "Socrates stands," my assent is evident — not by another's report, but by my own sense. Likewise when I assent to "man is an animal," the assent is evident because by my own intellect I perceive that a sensitive nature is in man. Even if no one asserted it — even if all asserted the contrary — I would still judge that proposition true.

7. Assent is inevident when someone assents not because sense or solid reason demonstrates the proposition true, but either because a light reason persuades it (a light reason does not drive away the mind's darkness, and so leaves the assent obscure and inevident) or because another testifies that it is true. He who has seen Peter slain and assents to "Peter is slain" has evident assent; he who assents only because of that man's narration has inevident assent, because neither sense nor reason shows him that it is true.

8. These three degrees so stand that the second includes the first and adds something; the third includes both and adds something further. For firmness it is enough that the foundation appear certain and solid to the one assenting. Even if in reality it is not such, if it appears such he will assent firmly and without hesitation. So heretics firmly assent to their errors: though their foundations are neither certain nor solid, to them — such is their blindness — they seem most efficacious and valid.

9. For certainty, and freedom from error, more is required: the foundation must not only appear certain and solid to the one assenting, but really and in itself be such. Otherwise the assent is erroneous and false. We may grant heretics firmness in judging; we do not grant them certainty of judging. Certainty and error cannot stand together.

10. For evidence still more is required: the foundation must appear certain and solid, and be such in itself — and it must not be another's testimony or narration, but either sense or some solid reason that clearly demonstrates that the matter so holds.

11. Assent can therefore be firm without being certain — as in heretics who without fear assent to dogmas that conflict with the Catholic faith or with good morals. Assent can also be certain without being evident. He who assents to a proposition because of God's testimony in Sacred Scripture has assent that is without doubt very certain, resting on the most certain foundation — God's own testimony — yet it is not evident. The theologian does not assent because sense or reason shows him that the matter so holds, but because God asserts or says that it so holds.

12. These three degrees of perfection in the mind's assent therefore stand so that the first extends more widely than the second, and the second than the third — just as among the degrees of necessity the "in a respect" sense extends more widely than the "in itself" sense, and that more widely than the "in itself primarily."

title: How knowing, believing, and opining differ from one another
english: Article II. How knowing, believing, and opining differ from one another.

1. Every assent of the mind is an act of knowing, of believing, or of opining. Whenever we judge something true, either we certainly know it, or we believe it because of another's testimony, or we opine it because of a light and inefficacious reason.

2. The act of knowing, opposed to believing and opining, is taken broadly for any actual certain and evident knowledge. Science so taken appears not only in speculative disciplines but in practical ones. In moral philosophy we do not opine or believe but evidently know that acts of liberality are honorable and the opposed vices dishonorable. Skilled architects do not opine or believe but evidently know that foundations must be set to the level and columns to the perpendicular. This knowledge concerns singulars as well as universals: when I see Peter standing or hear him speaking, I do not opine or believe — I know that he speaks and stands.

3. The division is sufficient: every assent rests either on testimony or on reason. If on testimony, it is actual faith — an act of believing. If on reason, either on certain and solid reason (science) or on merely probable reason (opinion).
4. Assent on another's testimony is either divine faith (on divine testimony) or human faith (on human testimony), as the Scholastics speak.

5. Note the Papists' error in passing. They grant with us that faith resting chiefly on men's testimony is human, not divine; yet they boldly claim that our assent to the articles of faith and to Scripture itself rests on the testimony of the "representative" Church — bishops and pastors in general council — and of the "virtual" Church, the Roman Pontiff. They must either confess that all wayfarers' faith is human (divine faith abolished) or call their bishops not men but gods.

6. Compare science, opinion, and divine faith. Science is firm, certain, and evident assent. Divine faith is firm and certain, but not evident. Opinion is sometimes firm (without hesitation), yet often neither firm nor certain nor evident.

7. Science is firm because the knower assents without doubt or hesitation; certain because he rests on a solid foundation — else he would opine, not know; evident because he assents not because another testifies, but because by some evident argument he himself perceives that the matter so holds.

8. Divine faith is firm because believers in God do not hesitate about sacred history and the divine promises; certain because it rests on God's testimony, who is truth itself; yet not evident — for the believer assents not because sense or reason shows him that the matter so holds, but because God testifies and asserts it.

9. So the Apostle in Hebrews 11:1 excellently expressed divine faith's nature: calling it hypostasis he marks its firmness and certainty; calling it the evidence of things not seen he declares its inevidence and enigmatic obscurity.

10. Opinion can sometimes be firm — people take light reasons for strongest arguments and assent without fear of the opposite — but it is never certain or evident. The one who opines rests on light reasons or men's testimonies, which never yield certainty or evidence of judging.

11. Does this comparison derogate from faith's dignity, since any science would then be a more perfect assent than faith for want of evidence? Answer: science is more perfect than faith in a respect, because it is evident assent; but faith is more perfect than any science simply and absolutely — for two reasons. First, faith concerns the noblest object: that great mystery of godliness — God revealed in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen by angels, preached to the nations. Second, faith rests on the most certain foundation: God's own testimony, who is truth itself and can neither deceive nor be deceived.

title: Whether faith is always the evidence of things not seen
english: Article III. Whether faith is always the evidence of things not seen.

1. The previous article showed that every faith — divine or human — is inevident assent. Hence the Apostle in Hebrews 11:1 calls faith the evidence of things not seen. The same is confirmed by 1 Corinthians 13:12 (we now see through a glass, in an enigma) and by the Apostle's teaching that faith will cease and be evacuated in the homeland — not perfected, as charity is — because obscurity and inevidence belong to faith's very notion and essence. So Augustine on John 14 ("I go to prepare a place for you"): let the Lord go that he may prepare a place; go that he may be seen, be hidden that he may be believed. Gregory likewise: appearances have not faith but recognition; what cannot be seen is truly said to be believed.

2. To make this plainer I will solve arguments that put even seen or known things under faith's object. First, the Lord's word in John 14: I have told you before it comes to pass, that when it is come to pass you may believe — as if faith were sometimes of things known by experience and so seen.
3. Next John 20: Thomas said, unless I see I will not believe (Christ risen); the Lord said to him already believing, because you have seen me, Thomas, you have believed.

4. Third: the other Apostles, the Virgin Mary, and many faithful believed what they saw — Christ as man, suffered, dead, buried, risen, ascended, and much else in the articles of faith. So 1 John: what we have heard, seen with our eyes, looked upon, and handled of the word of life, we announce to you.

5. Fourth: a philosopher who knows by demonstration that one God is principle and cause of all can, becoming a Christian from a pagan, receive faith of the same proposition while the prior cognition remains — and so have faith and science together, faith having for object things evidently known or seen.

6. To remove these arguments I first set foundations, then confute Fonseca, Estius, and others on the supposed repugnance of faith and science. First: "faith" or "to believe" is often taken in Scripture and among approved authors for assenting in any way that something is true — as when one "believes his eyes," or dialecticians say an argument "makes faith."

7. Second: St Thomas and the other Apostles and faithful saw one thing and believed another — a man seen, God believed. Augustine: they beheld a living man whom they had seen dying, and believed God hidden in the flesh; a man appeared among men, offering man to those who see, keeping God for those who believe.

8. Third: faith is called inevident assent and the evidence of things not seen — not because the things believed are altogether unseen, but because insofar as they are believed they lack evidence from that on account of which they are believed. Science's foundation (the middle of demonstration) convinces by the thing's evidence, opening causes; faith's foundation (God's authority) convinces by its certainty and infallibility, not by the evidence of the thing assented to. Faith's office is not to make obscure things clear, but to make the intellect yield to the speaker's authority. So things believed, as believed, are inevident (see Pareus; Field). Yet they may be evident in another respect — to sense or reason. One proposition can be necessary as a demonstration's conclusion and contingent as a probable syllogism's; so certain articles of faith have clarity insofar as the Apostles perceived them by sense or we demonstrate them by reason, but insofar as they are believed because of God's testifying authority they lack that evidence and are rightly called things not seen.

title: Whether faith can coexist with science of the same proposition in the same intellect
english: Article IV. Whether faith can coexist with science of the same proposition in the same intellect.

1. The question is whether one and the same person can at once believe and know the proposition to which he assents, or whether faith and science so repugn that they cannot coexist in one intellect. Opinions diverge so widely that two celebrated men scarcely agree. Scotus holds that neither act nor habit of faith and of science can coexist in the same intellect about the same subject.

2. Durandus holds the contrary: faith and science can coexist about the same proposition in the same intellect, as to both act and habit. Fonseca: the habits can coexist about the same subject, yet the act produced is not an act of faith but a certain supernatural science, because faith concurs in producing it. Estius: (1) the habits can coexist about the same object; (2) each can exercise its act at different times; (3) the act the habit of faith then elicits is not faith in the full amplitude of its meaning — not according to all required conditions — because it is not inevident knowledge of the thing.

3. The fifth and truest view is Antonio Rubio's: (1) these habits can be together in the same intellect about the same object; (2) each can exercise its act at different times, but not at the same time; (3) acts elicited at different times are true and proper acts of those habits, and the habit of knowing derogates nothing from the act of believing. Rubio speaks there of science and opinion, but the same reason holds for science and faith.

4. Against Scotus: the habits can coexist. What would impede them is chiefly repugnance of their acts — but that does not impede. Habits are easy potencies for acts; we can have at once potencies for repugnant acts exercised at different times (weeping and laughing, walking and sitting) though not both acts at once. Further: one who by faith knows God created the world can later acquire demonstrative science of creation without destroying that faith — else a Christian could not study metaphysics and physics, from which such demonstrations are gathered, and one may not do what destroys or diminishes faith.

5. Against Durandus: the intellect cannot in one and the same instant elicit both faith's inevident assent and science's evident assent. As sight cannot see the same thing at once distinctly and confusedly, so the intellect (the soul's eye) cannot perceive the same thing at once evidently and inevidently.

6. Against Fonseca and Estius: even while coexisting with the habit of science, the habit of faith can elicit a true and proper act of faith with all conditions required for believing — so faith and science can be in the same intellect about the same proposition as to acts, but elicited at different times. A believer, even after acquiring science of creation, can resolve: I so firmly assent that God created the world because of God's testifying authority that even if reason did not show it — even if corrupt reason said the contrary — I would still assent without fear.

7. That judgment comes from faith alone, not from science and faith together, and is a true act of faith. Neither science nor any natural habit can dictate such a resolve. The assent rests on the testifier's authority alone and is inevident: a foundation that yields certainty but not evidence makes the assent inevident; God's authority convinces by certainty and irrefragability, not by the thing's clarity. As the medium is, so is the assent — certain or uncertain, evident or inevident.

title: On the division of faith into explicit and implicit; and whether the inevidence we ascribe to faith favors the blind and implicit faith of the Papists
english: Article V. On the division of faith into explicit and implicit; and whether the inevidence we ascribe to faith favors the blind and implicit faith of the Papists.

1. Theologians divide faith into explicit and implicit — Lombard's distinct and veiled or confused (Tilenus, Durandus, Thomas, Estius). Explicit faith believes something distinctly in itself and in particular. Implicit faith believes something not in itself but in another, as in a universal. Simpler Christians who grasp only what is absolutely necessary to salvation — articles, Decalogue, and the like — when they sincerely hold Scripture to be God's word and worthy of faith, believe that general object explicitly, and believe particular histories and dogmas of Scripture (Noah's three sons, Abraham's two, the scepter not taken from Judah before the Messiah) implicitly and by consequence in that general. Those who believe the whole Scripture true have implicit faith of all its histories, dogmas, and prophecies whose distinct knowledge they have not yet acquired.

2. May Reformed schools admit this division? First assertion: yes, if soundly conceived. Not only laypeople but the most learned theologians believe some things implicitly under the general that Scripture is God's word — things they have not yet distinctly understood. Daily progress in knowing Scripture shows not Scripture's obscurity (as Papists claim) but our mind's weakness and the immense wealth of heavenly mysteries poured little by little into the narrow vessel of the human mind.

3. Second assertion: taken as the Papists take it, the division is crude, absurd, and contrary to faith's nature. Their "implicit faith" is laypeople believing unknown dogmas under the general that whatever the Roman Church believes is true. That is human faith, not divine — resting on men's testimony, not God's; a light conjecture on a fragile foundation, not hypostasis or elenchos.

4. Does the inevidence Orthodox doctors ascribe to faith favor that blind Papist faith? That confused assent on Rome's testimony alone is most inevident — yet inevidence does not help them. It excludes only scientific knowledge (sense or evident reason from the thing's nature), not all knowledge. Certainty, faith's second condition, presupposes firm persuasion that what we assent to is God's word, not man's. That persuasion is opposed to Papist implicit faith; certainty cannot be found in it.
