title: On the threefold light: of nature, of faith or grace, and of glory
english: Article VI. On the threefold light: of nature, of faith or grace, and of glory.

1. Scholastic theology draws several distinctions from nature, grace, and glory. First: God's kingdom — of nature (his empire over all creatures), of grace (reign in the Church militant), and of glory (reign in the Church triumphant).
2. Second: God's presence — natural or essential (everywhere), gracious (in the just, who are his temple), and glorious (in heaven, manifesting majesty to the blessed).

3. Third: works ad extra — of nature (creation, conservation, cooperation — in him we live and move and are); of grace (the Word's incarnation, humiliation, exaltation, threefold office; effectual calling, regeneration, justification, sanctification); of glory (the elect's glorification and the reprobate's damnation).
4. Fourth: human life — natural (animal and rational), of grace (spiritual life to God by faith and charity), and of glory (seeing God face to face in the homeland).
5. Fifth: God's decree as ordering things of nature, grace, and glory.

6. Sixth, and most to our purpose: the mind's light — of nature (fallen man's power to grasp self-evident principles and natural conclusions); of faith or grace (supernatural illumination believing what Scripture reveals above natural reason); of glory (the blessed's naked, intuitive vision of God).
7. Faith's light stands between nature and glory: above nature (loftier objects, surer foundation), below glory (not intuition but inevident assent on God's testimony).

8. Papists invent a further "prophetic" light by which Church doctors — especially the Roman Pontiff — judge faith infallibly. Scripture does not support it; it shifts wayfarers' faith from God's word to men's judgments.

title: Whether there is given to wayfarers any light clearer than the light of faith
english: Article VII. Whether there is given to wayfarers any light clearer than the light of faith.

1. Theology divides into wayfarers' and comprehensors' — of the way and of the homeland. The first rests on faith's light; the second on glory's. Is any clearer light given to wayfarers so that they know faith's mysteries evidently?

2. Papists and some Scholastics posit a prophetic light or gift of understanding by which Church doctors judge mysteries more clearly than ordinary believers. The Orthodox deny any light clearer than faith as to the thing's evidence — though faith's own light may admit degrees of extension and firmness.

3. Faith's notion involves inevidence. A clearer light that made faith's objects evident would turn them into objects of science or vision. In the way there is not vision of God but faith: we walk by faith, not by sight (2 Corinthians 5:7).

4. That learned theologians grasp and explain more credibles comes from greater learning, Scripture study, and ministerial gifts for edification — not from a light above faith. Those gifts do not remove inevidence or make mysteries seen.
5. No light clearer than faith as to the mode of knowing is given to wayfarers. Glory's light belongs only to comprehensors in the homeland.

title: Three questions solved: whether faith is well divided into infused and acquired; whether faith is more certain than the sciences; what it is properly to believe in God
english: Article VIII. Three questions solved: whether faith is well divided into infused and acquired; whether faith is more certain than the sciences; what it is properly to believe in God.

1. Infused vs acquired. Scholastics distinguish faith God creates by grace in the soul from faith gained by study and teaching. The Orthodox grant historical or acquired faith — even in demons and hypocrites — but deny that justifying, saving faith is acquired. It is God's gift, infused by the Spirit, not born of human industry.

2. Is faith more certain than the sciences? Divine faith is more certain than any created science — not as to evidence (science is evident; faith inevident), but as to the foundation's firmness. Faith rests on God's testimony, who can neither deceive nor be deceived; the sciences rest on created middles that, however certain, do not equal God's infallibility.

3. What is it properly to believe in God? Distinguish: believing that God is; believing God (what he says); and believing in God — resting trustingly on God as salvation's author. That last is proper to justifying faith and does not belong to demons, who believe and tremble.

title: The opinion of Nicolaas Grevinchoven is refuted — that the habit of faith is not infused but acquired
english: Article IX. The opinion of Nicolaas Grevinchoven is refuted — that the habit of faith is not infused but acquired.

1. Grevinchoven, a Remonstrant, holds that faith's habit is not infused by God but acquired by using the means and hearing the word diligently — as arts and sciences are acquired. The Orthodox reject this.
2. Scripture calls faith God's gift, not a human work (Ephesians 2:8; Philippians 1:29 — it has been granted to you to believe in Christ).
3. Justifying faith is supernatural; its objects surpass nature's grasp. It cannot be acquired by nature's powers; it needs God's infusion and the Spirit's operation.

5. Grevinchoven's view opens onto Pelagianism and Arminianism, giving man power to believe from himself without special prevenient and operating grace. It is to be rejected.

title: Whether actual or habitual faith is in infants, or can be in them
english: Article X. Whether actual or habitual faith is in infants, or can be in them.

1. First: it is not absolutely impossible for infants to have both actual and habitual faith. Habitual faith is plain enough — in integrity infants would have been born with supernatural habits; in corruption God can create faith's habit in their souls by the Spirit, as in adults.

2. Actual faith is harder. Some deny infants any intellective acts. Others, with Augustine and many Orthodox, grant that God can elicit in them hidden, ineffable acts of faith in a manner known to himself — especially in baptism, where the Spirit works in covenanted infants.

3. Second: possibility does not bind us to assert that every baptized infant actually has faith. Covenanted infants' salvation rests on God's promise and Christ's merit, not on a demonstrable act of faith in them.

4. Third: parents' or the Church's faith is not formally the infants' faith. The Papist fiction of alien faith imputed to infants is rejected. Covenanted infants are saved by God's grace in Christ — baptism its sign and seal — not by alien faith as a formal principle in them.
5. In adults both habitual and actual faith are required for justification: habit as principle, act as the exercise that apprehends Christ.

title: How that Remonstrant argument is to be solved: that whatever each is bound to believe is true
english: Article XV. How that Remonstrant argument is to be solved: that whatever each is bound to believe is true.

2. Orthodox answers: deny the major, distinguish the minor, or deny the minor. Denying the major is unsafe — as if God commanded the reprobate to believe falsehoods.

3. Safer: the precept to believe Christ died for you does not bind absolutely without condition, but under conversion and repentance. Those who own their sins and sorrow for them are commanded to believe Christ died for them.

4. The reprobate are not bound to believe they are elect, or that Christ died for them as they remain in malice; they are bound to convert and believe the Gospel. The unbelief that damns is refractory impenitence, not mere denial of historical assent.
5. So the sophism falls, and particular satisfaction for the elect stands with the Gospel's universal proclamation.

title: Whether faith is a discursive assent; and whether the Papists use a circular discourse in establishing faith
english: Article XVI. Whether faith is a discursive assent; and whether the Papists use a circular discourse in establishing faith.
1. Assent is simple — to propositions clear by their own light — or discursive — to a conclusion because of premises.
2. Divine faith is discursive: we assent to the articles because God has spoken, or Scripture testifies. It is not simple noetic assent; faith's mysteries are not self-evident to nature's light.
3. Papists establish faith by a vicious circle: Scripture is God's word because the Church says so; the Church is infallible because Scripture says so. That tends to destroy divine faith.
4. Orthodox deny the circle. Faith's principle is God's word authenticating itself by intrinsic marks and the Spirit's internal testimony — not Rome's authority as first foundation.

title: Whether knowledge is an act elicited from the habit of faith
english: Article XVII. Whether knowledge is an act elicited from the habit of faith.
1. Bellarmine says faith is assent, not knowledge — knowledge only a prerequisite, not faith's own act.
2. Distinguish: knowledge of terms; of the proposition as proposed; and the judgment by which we assent. The first two precede faith's assent; the third is assent itself or joined to it.
3. Justifying faith is not bare historical knowledge but fiducial assent. If Bellarmine severs faith from knowledge entirely, reject that. Orthodox: faith includes knowledge, assent, and trust.

title: Whether trust is an act of faith
english: Article XVIII. Whether trust is an act of faith.
1. Orthodox theologians differ on trust: some identify it with faith's justifying act; some call it distinct but inseparable; some take trust in several senses.
2. Trust may mean: firm persuasion of God's mercy in Christ; resting on his promises; courageous stance against dangers and miseries; or joy and peace of conscience over remission already obtained.

3. With most Orthodox: justifying trust is an act of faith — or justifying faith essentially includes the trust by which Christ and grace's promises are applied to us. Not mere historical knowledge or bare dogmatic assent.
4. Bellarmine's claim that certainty of particular remission needs special revelation in this life is rejected. Scripture urges trust and gives the regenerate signs of their share in Christ.

title: Whether trust is an act of the intellect, and how it differs from assent
english: Article XIX. Whether trust is an act of the intellect, and how it differs from assent.
1. Is trust in the intellect or the will? Roman Catholics commonly place it in the will. Orthodox distinguish.

2. As firm persuasion about God's promise, trust is an intellective act — not really distinct from faith's assent, but in reason: assent regards the testimony's truth; trust regards the promised good as applicable to me.
3. As loving motion and the will's resting on God, trust is a will-act — inseparable from faith in the justified, formally distinct.
4. Middle Orthodox view: justifying faith as assent and persuasion is in the intellect as proper subject; it belongs to the will by origin (will-commanded), concomitance (charity), and fruits.

title: Whether the object of saving faith is remission of sins already obtained, or remission to be obtained
english: Article XX. Whether the object of saving faith is remission of sins already obtained, or remission to be obtained.
1. Is justifying faith's object remission already had, or Christ and the promise of remission through faith?

2. With the Orthodox: the primary object is Christ the Mediator and God's promise in him. Faith justifies not by believing remission already formally inheres, but by apprehending Christ, in whom remission is offered and by faith applied.

3. Bellarmine: if faith were trust of particular remission already had, it would presuppose the justification it causes. Solved: faith does not presuppose remission as inhering before faith; it follows and applies it. The object is the promise and Christ — not remission as prior possession.

title: Whether and how far faith belongs to the will
english: Article XXI. Whether and how far faith belongs to the will.
1. Estius puts faith with the will; others put it wholly in the intellect. We distinguish.

2. As assent and judgment, faith is in the intellect as proper subject. It still belongs to the will: by origin (the will commands the intellect to attend and assent); by state (faith directs the will); by fruits (love, trust, obedience born from faith in the will).
3. Unlike Estius, we do not seat faith in the will by origin alone, but relate it to the will by command, concomitance, and fruits.

title: Whether charity is the form of faith
english: Article XXII. Whether charity is the form of faith.
1. Papists, after some Scholastics, make charity faith's form — faith without charity unformed and dead, formed by charity unto justification.

2. Orthodox reject this. Justifying faith is not shaped by charity as an extrinsic accidental form. Living fiducial faith justifies before charity formally considered — though charity inseparably accompanies living faith.
3. Dead (merely historical) faith is not the same kind as justifying faith. It needs not charity to "form" it, but the regenerating Spirit to make it living.

title: Whether religion is a theological virtue distinct from faith

title: Against Antonio Rubio: that theology in the second sense is not science but divine faith
english: Article XXV. Against Antonio Rubio: that theology in the second sense is not science but divine faith.
1. Rubio calls theology (deducing from faith's principles) true science. We deny it.

2. Aristotelian science rests on self-evident, evidently seen principles. Theology's principles (articles of faith) are believed, not seen. Discourse from them yields discursive faith — a faithful conclusion — not science properly so called.
3. Theology may be called science broadly, or wisdom — not Aristotelian science strictly.

title: That theology in the third sense — scholastic theology — is an aggregate habit from faith and the philosophical disciplines
english: Article XXVI. That theology in the third sense — scholastic theology — is an aggregate habit from faith and the philosophical disciplines.

2. So it is not a simple habit but an aggregate of faith and philosophical habits: logic for arguments, metaphysics for being and causes, ethics for the Decalogue's virtues and vices.

title: That theology is like all the Aristotelian habits, and especially like prudence
english: Article XXVII. That theology resembles every Aristotelian intellectual habit — and prudence most of all.

1. Taken broadly, theology is compared to Aristotle's five intellectual habits (understanding, science, wisdom, art, prudence). The point is analogy of office in theology's own order, not identity with those habits.

2. The closest likeness is prudence. Prudence steers human action toward an end; theology steers mind and life toward the supernatural end — God's glory and eternal salvation — by the norms God has revealed.

title: Whether true and properly so-called theology can be in an ungodly human being
english: Article XXX. Whether true and properly so-called theology can be in an ungodly human being.
1. Can an ungodly person — hypocrite, heretic, or merely learned — have true theology?
2. As bare historical knowledge of articles and scholastic conclusions: yes. Demons and hypocrites know many true things about God.
3. As saving wisdom — living faith with fear of God and obedience: no. That theology is the Spirit's gift, inseparable from charity and saving faith.
4. Conclusion: theology properly so called is not in the ungodly; acquired theological knowledge and faith's history may be. End of the Third Exercise.
